newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's MOF scuppers credit union bailout plan.
newsitem.headline: Japan's MOF scuppers credit union bailout plan.

text.p: Japan's Finance Ministry has scuppered plans by a local authority in western Japan to bail out troubled credit unions, saying it will not go back to its old ways of protecting the weak.

An Osaka prefecture official said on Tuesday that the local government there had been forced to shelve a proposed rescue scheme after the Ministry of Finance (MOF) refused to back the move and ruled out providing any funds.

"The MOF stuck to its position that it now respects the voluntary will of private banks and that it will deal with such issues with more transparency," said Toshimichi Oi, Osaka prefecture's executive director in charge of credit unions.

The ministry's resolutely "laissez faire" stance left the Osaka prefectural government no option but to give up the plan after failing to secure the ministry's endorsement in time for a council budget deadline on Tuesday.

Under the scheme, several troubled credit unions were to merge and set up a new entity after transferring their bad loans to the Resolution and Collection Bank, a body set up last year to manage and collect loans left by failed credit unions.

"The (rescue) plan, drawn up last September, was supposed to come in time for presentation at the Osaka council session," Oi said. "But we will have to put it off due to several unresolved issues," he said.

Under Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's "Big Bang" financial liberalisation plans, banks and other financial institutions in poor health would no longer be able to ask for the government's protection.

Japan last year budgeted 685 billion yen ($5.61 billion) in tax money to help wind up failed mortgage firms, but said no further public money should be used to deal with bad loans held at similar financial institutions.
Credit unions take deposits and lend mainly to members and are supervised by local governments.
The Osaka government had hoped the Finance Ministry would take a lead in the bailout as it has in the past, by helping to fund the new financial entity.

Officials also said they had counted on the ministry to act as an intermediary between the failed credit unions and their rescue partners -- usually large city banks -- which would take over what assets were left from a government-led liquidation.
Earlier this year, assets of the failed Osaka Credit Union were passed on to Tokai Bank through MOF guidance.
But this time, the government has insisted that market forces must take their course, Osaka officials said. They also said the Bank of Japan had refused to provide funds.

The Osaka government is now hoping Sanwa Bank will step in to help clear up the mess left by Kizu Credit Union, which collapsed last August, on the grounds the two had close business ties in the past.
But officials said that since the collapse of Hanwa Bank last year, the ministry had been reluctant to call on Japan's private banks to help clean up others' failures.

Last November, the Finance Ministry ordered Hanwa, also based in western Japan, to suspend most of its business because it was unable to recover on its bad loans. It was the first suspension of a Japanese bank in five decades.
Hanwa last month filed an objection to the forced suspension, saying that it did not guarantee jobs for the 850 employees at the bank.
"The MOF scheme is a far cry from protecting our employees," a Hanwa spokesman said.

But a source at the local branch of MOF said such protection was not the purpose of the plan. "The objection will likely be dismissed soon. We cannot set a precedent when Japan's financial reforms are just beginning," the source said.
